narrowest_regime: full-rank design matrix, fixed set of terms; sequential (Type I) sums of squares and which of two exactly-collinear columns is aliased do depend on order
reason: The OLS coefficient of any column is X_j' M_{-j} y / X_j' M_{-j} X_j with M_{-j} the residual-maker of the other columns, which is unchanged by permuting columns; the residual variance, SE, t and p are likewise invariant, so only sequential SS depend on order. In a rank-deficient design the aliased column does depend on order, but that is not the stated regime.
bite_note: Not asking about predictor order loses nothing; asking would not change any reported estimate, interval or p-value.

failing_part: bootstrap optimism correction is the recommended default (ahead of repeated cross-validation), stated for any learner at clinical sample sizes
narrowest_regime: pre-specified or penalized regression-type models (logistic/linear/Cox) with the whole fitting pipeline re-run in each resample; there the ranking single split weakest is well supported and bootstrap vs repeated CV is near a tie
reason: Steyerberg 2001 and Austin & Steyerberg 2017 show split-sample is inefficient and bootstrap is good for logistic regression, but Smith 2014 finds repeated CV, bootstrap and leave-pair-out comparably unbiased, and Iba 2021 finds Harrell's correction biased in small samples. In my simulation (n=150, 8 predictors, true AUC about 0.63) Harrell's bootstrap correction for a random forest returned AUC 0.94 against a true 0.63 (apparent AUC 1.0, in-bag rows leak into the original-sample test), while repeated 5-fold CV returned 0.62; for logistic regression both were within 0.01. So a bootstrap-first default is wrong for flexible learners, which the app fits.

citations.cite: Steyerberg EW et al., J Clin Epidemiol 2001;54:774-781
Austin PC, Steyerberg EW, Stat Methods Med Res 2017;26:796-808
Smith GC et al., Am J Epidemiol 2014;180:318-324
Iba K et al., BMC Med Res Methodol 2021;21:9

bite_note: Sets which scheme is first on the seal card; for forests or boosted trees a bootstrap-optimism default would report a grossly optimistic score where repeated CV would not.

failing_part: covariate adjustment only sharpens precision; a case-control sample cannot give prevalence or absolute risk; matched sets are analyzed within each set
narrowest_regime: Adjustment only sharpens precision for collapsible effect measures (difference in means via linear model) with balanced allocation and modest covariate count; absolute risk is unobtainable only when sampling fractions are unknown; within-set analysis is needed for individually matched sets, not frequency matching
reason: For non-collapsible measures (odds ratio, hazard ratio) adjusting in a randomized trial changes the estimand: in my simulation a randomized treatment with a prognostic covariate gave unadjusted OR 1.85 versus adjusted OR 2.76, with a larger SE, so it is not precision only; with unequal allocation or small trials adjustment can also lose precision (Freedman 2008). A case-control sample with known sampling fractions or an external incidence (population-based, case-cohort, nested designs) does support absolute risk. Frequency-matched samples do not require set-wise analysis.

citations.cite: Hauck WW, Neuhaus JM, Kalbfleisch JD, Anderson S. J Clin Epidemiol 1991;44:77-81 (omitted covariates and odds ratios)
Freedman DA, Adv Appl Math 2008;40:180-193 (regression adjustment in experiments)
Greenland S, Robins JM, Pearl J. Stat Sci 1999;14:29-46 (collapsibility)

bite_note: Gates whether adjusted and unadjusted effects are presented as the same quantity in a randomized logistic or Cox analysis, and whether absolute-risk wording is refused for case-control data.

failing_part: because it penalizes predictions that are systematically too high or too low ... the conservative choice over 1 - SSE/SST
narrowest_regime: none; squared Pearson correlation is the R-squared of the best linear recalibration of the predictions, so it is at least 1 - SSE/SST and ignores bias and scale error
reason: The squared correlation is invariant to any affine transformation of the predictions, so it does not penalize systematic over- or under-prediction at all; 1 - SSE/SST does. In my simulation predictions shifted by +2 or scaled by 3 left r^2 at 0.489 while 1 - SSE/SST fell to -1.57 and -1.65. Kvalseth 1985 cautions against r^2 for non-OLS fits and favors 1 - SSE/SST. The claim states the opposite of the truth and the cited paper does not support it.

citations.cite: Kvalseth TO, Am Stat 1985;39:279-285 (not indexed in Europe PMC; content from memory)

bite_note: For cross-validated predictions from over-fit or shrunk models the reported R-squared would be positive and flattering where 1 - SSE/SST is negative or near zero.

failing_part: is an outcome-blind predictor ... good enough to band the noticing
narrowest_regime: as a coarse rank signal when removed rows differ from kept rows in ways that carry through to the exposure-outcome slope; not as a calibrated predictor in half-width units
reason: Selection on covariates that the model adjusts for does not bias the adjusted coefficient, so a large SMD on the adjustment set can coexist with no movement; conversely differential exposure error in the removed rows moves the estimate without a large SMD on the adjusters. The proxy also has no n in it, yet movement in half-width units scales with sqrt(n) for fixed bias. In my dietary-style simulation (1,688 scenarios, energy range rule, differential reporting error) the Spearman correlation of share x max SMD with the shift was 0.34 (0.18 without energy), the product's median was constant across n=500, 2000, 8000 while the median shift rose 0.11, 0.18, 0.36 half-widths, and within one product bin the shift spanned about 0.01 to 0.8. Nine calibration cases cannot validate a banding rule.

citations.cite: Austin PC, Stat Med 2009;28:3083-3107 (SMD defined for balance of treatment groups, not as a predictor of estimate shift)

bite_note: Sets the predicted band and the recommended triage disposition (keep, flag, act); a coarse proxy can mis-band by an order of magnitude for a given n.

failing_part: its nutrient coefficient is the standard model's exactly, because the residual and total energy span the same model as the nutrient and total energy
narrowest_regime: exactly equal only if the outcome model also contains the stratum indicator and the stratum x energy interaction (or the within-stratum slopes happen to be identical in the sample)
reason: The within-stratum residual is r = N - a_s - b_s*E with stratum-specific a_s and b_s, so N = r + a_s + b_s*E needs stratum and stratum x E terms to lie in the span; with only r and E (or r, E, stratum) the spans differ. In my simulation the standard coefficient was 0.0743 (Y~N+E) against 0.0979 for the residual model, 0.0963 vs 0.0979 with a stratum main effect, and identical (0.09788) only once stratum and stratum x E were added. The pooled-residual identity does not carry over to strata.

citations.cite: McCullough ML, Byrd DA, Am J Epidemiol 2023 (residual method with energy in model)

bite_note: The app's estimand sentence would tell a researcher the stratified residual coefficient is the standard model's nutrient effect; it is a different, stratum-weighted quantity unless the interaction terms are in the model.

failing_part: at least 10 events estimates the C-statistic and the calibration slope precisely enough to be useful, so a held-out score is offered from 10 events
narrowest_regime: Collins et al. recommend at least 100 events (and 100 non-events), ideally 200 or more, for external validation
reason: The cited paper concludes that validating a prognostic model needs a minimum of 100 events, ideally 200+. My simulation of a calibrated model with 10 events (n=100) gave an AUC SD of 0.07 (about +/-0.14) and a calibration slope SD of 0.39 (5-95% range 0.52 to 1.80, true value 1); at 100 events the SDs were 0.02 and 0.10. At 10 events neither measure is precise enough to be useful.

citations.cite: Collins GS, Ogundimu EO, Altman DG, Stat Med 2016;35:214-226

bite_note: Sets the minimum held-out size; offering a score from 10 events instead of withholding or warning leads researchers to report an AUC and slope whose intervals span most of the plausible range.

failing_part: more than 10 repeating values, or one value per row, is a unit structure (as licence to cluster intervals); the 3 and 10 cut points
narrowest_regime: the lower rule holds: with fewer than 3 distinct values a column cannot be a unit identifier and cluster-robust intervals by it are invalid; the upper cut of 10 is a convention
reason: Fewer than 3 clusters really is invalid (my simulation: cluster-robust 95% interval coverage 0.54 normal, 0.90 t at G=2). But 10 is borrowed from a category-level cap, not from inference: at G=11 coverage was 0.89 (normal) or 0.92 (t), at G=5 0.81 or 0.92, G=30 0.92 or 0.94, so a column just over 10 repeating values still gives anti-conservative clustered intervals unless a small-cluster correction is applied. A one-value-per-row column forms singleton clusters, which adds no dependence structure (it reduces to a robust-variance interval).

citations.cite: Cameron AC, Gelbach JB, Miller DL, Rev Econ Stat 2008;90:414-427 (few clusters)

bite_note: Decides whether a column may cluster the intervals or group the seal, and whether an interval is refused; the 11-to-40 unit range is where the app would cluster but coverage is below nominal.

narrowest_regime: Sufficiency holds: if the chance of being a complete case is independent of the outcome given the covariates, complete-case coefficients are unbiased. Necessity fails.
reason: White & Carlin show the sufficient direction; they do not claim necessity. For logistic regression complete-case slopes stay unbiased when missingness depends on the outcome but not on the exposure given the outcome and other covariates (Bartlett, Harel & Carpenter 2015). In my simulation, with missingness depending only on y, the logistic slope was 0.703 (true 0.70) while the intercept was biased; a linear regression under the same dependence gave 0.508 (true 0.70). So outcome dependence is not always fatal, and the stated regime includes logistic and Cox.

citations.cite: White IR, Carlin JB, Stat Med 2010;29:2920-2931
Bartlett JW, Harel O, Carpenter JR, Am J Epidemiol 2015;182:730-736
Groenwold RHH et al., CMAJ 2012;184:1265-1269 (exists; the content for the iff claim not checked)

bite_note: The assumption written into the record and methods sentence would warn a logistic-regression user off a valid complete-case analysis, or lead them to treat a violated sufficient condition as proof of bias.

narrowest_regime: metabolomics with pooled QC samples; the wording that 50 percent leaves too little biological variance is loose (at D=50% the biological variance is still 3 times the technical)
reason: Broadhurst 2018 defines D-ratio = SD of pooled QC / SD of study samples x 100% and recommends an acceptance criterion of at most < 50% (preferably much lower), so the filter and threshold match the source. The filter uses no outcome, so computing the study SD within each training fold is a conservative way to avoid using held-out rows, and the QC SD comes from separate samples so freezing it is harmless. The cut is a convention, not an optimum.

citations.cite: Broadhurst D et al., Metabolomics 2018;14:72 (D-ratio definition and < 50% criterion read in PMC5960010)

bite_note: Removes noisy features from the model's inputs when chosen; the effect on prediction is usually small but the retained feature list changes.

failing_part: the estimate is 'mostly the tail' when the part above is more than half and its interval excludes zero
narrowest_regime: The exact additive split of the coefficient holds (linearity of OLS in y, same rows and design). The label is valid only if the above-cut share is compared with the fraction of people above the cut
reason: Because OLS is linear in y the two coefficients add exactly (my check: difference 1e-15). But under a pure uniform location shift the above-cut share equals P(y > c): with the cut at the 20th percentile the share was 0.78 with an interval excluding zero, so the rule says 'mostly the tail' for an effect that is the same for everyone. The share also is not meaningful when the parts have opposite signs or the total is near zero, and 'more than half' is not tested.
bite_note: Decides the wording of the typical-person-or-tail standing question; with a cut-off below the median it would label a uniform shift as tail-driven.

failing_part: enough to choose settings that predict at least as well as the standard settings
narrowest_regime: when the standard settings over-fit at that n (a weak default), 8 Sobol candidates helped; when the standard settings are already regularized, the search gives about zero average gain
reason: Random search being a strong baseline (low effective dimension) explains good coverage of the space, not that the choice among 9 configurations by noisy inner CV at n=300 beats a good default. In my simulation (gradient boosting, n=300, 8 candidates plus default) an over-fitting default (sklearn defaults) lost to the tuned choice by +0.025 to +0.033 AUC with 0 to 5% of datasets worse, but a regularized default gave +0.003 and -0.001 AUC (SE about 0.003) with 35 to 40% of datasets worse and one run with a worse log loss. The 8 / 16 sizes and the 300 / 1,000 cut points have no stated methods justification.

citations.cite: Bergstra J, Bengio Y, JMLR 2012;13:281-305 (random search; PDF could not be parsed here)
Probst P, Boulesteix A-L, Bischl B, JMLR 2019;20:1-32 (tunability)

bite_note: Whether the pipeline tunes and with how many candidates changes the fitted model; the gain is about 0.03 AUC against a weak default and about zero against a strong one, so the cost is not always repaid.

narrowest_regime: Best established for logistic regression; supported here by simulation for random forest and gradient boosting at about 5 percent prevalence
reason: van den Goorbergh et al. show undersampling, oversampling and SMOTE strongly overestimate the minority-class probability and do not improve discrimination, and that adjusting the threshold gives similar sensitivity and specificity. My simulation (prevalence 5%, n=2500) with class weighting gave mean predicted risk 0.41 (LR), 0.09 (RF) and 0.26 (GB) against a true 0.05, with AUC changes of +0.001, +0.004 and -0.025. A defaulting-off rule with a threshold move is the sound choice, though a flexible learner at extreme imbalance or tiny n could occasionally gain ranking from weighting.

citations.cite: van den Goorbergh R, van Smeden M, Timmerman D, Van Calster B, JAMIA 2022;29:1525-1534

bite_note: No resampling or weighting by default keeps predicted probabilities calibrated; the alternative of balancing would inflate risks several-fold and leave AUC unchanged or worse.
